This is an exact duplicate of the messenger-fit relation in macro:messenger_medium_fit. That finding also carries all nine HFT branch refs, supplied roles, focus returns, 17:94-95 context, and the attributed qualification; no branch, context, or obligation is excluded.

findings.title: The messenger fits the inhabited field
findings.claim: The human messenger rejected in 17:94 is shown as a fitting medium for human recipients: 17:95 matches an angel messenger to angels settled on earth, and 17:96 places the exchange under the witness who knows and sees His servants.
findings.mechanism: The carrier is the human messenger in 17:94; the independent counterfactual in 17:95 makes the receiver type explicit and pairs angel residents with an angel messenger. That contact changes human embodiment from the stated objection into a medium fitted to its receiving field. The focus sufficiency and witness terms frame the fit as an adequate answer. HFT before/after movement: before, God witnesses the messenger's truth despite ordinary embodiment; after, the witness certifies the human-human fit.
findings.reader_payoff: The human form can be read as part of how guidance reaches a human community, while God's witness answers the dispute without staging the requested spectacle.
findings.containment: The fit is a bounded reading of the explicit 17:94-95 counterfactual, not a universal rule that every recipient requires a messenger of its own kind. It does not displace the primary assertion that God is sufficient as witness. The HFT version remains attributed; an ordinary rebuttal of the angel demand remains live.

epistemic.reason: The trusted channel evidence and exact 17:94-96 surface support the receiver-medium relation. The legacy-unbound HFT contributes additional branch roles without target morphology, so the conclusion stays a contextual inference rather than an explicit universal rule.

findings.title: The saying carries a commissioned verdict
findings.claim: The repeated command to speak, first paired with a request for authority and then with the arrival of truth and disappearance of falsehood, lets the final qul be heard as a commissioned verdict backed by God's testimony.
findings.mechanism: The focus command qul is the carrier; 17:80 supplies an earlier commanded utterance and request for sultan, while 17:81 gives the truth/falsehood criterion. Their contact with the final shahid changes the focus from an improvised personal appeal into a publicly voiced, commissioned verdict. Before, the speaker asks God to corroborate him; after, the saying inherits verdict force from the sender-witness and the truth that stands.
findings.reader_payoff: The focus answer sounds like the continuation of a publicly authorized saying, not a fresh self-defense.
findings.containment: The cumulative movement is an attributed HFT reading. The earlier formulas may instead be parallel proclamations without a juridical sequence; the focus still commands a saying and names God as sufficient witness.

findings.title: The witness sees how the address meets its hearers
findings.claim: The same Qur'anic address yields trust for some and loss for others; the turning away and patterned action in 17:83-84 meet the focus pair of inner expertise and sight, so the final witness can be read as discerning uptake through inward disposition and outward conduct.
findings.mechanism: Before, the focus witness can be read as neutrally observing two parties. The context shows opposed effects of the Qur'an, a bodily turning away, and each person acting along a shaping pattern known to the Lord. Khabir and basir meet those separate inward and outward signals; after, witness becomes diagnostic of how the same address is received, without selecting which contextual reading is true.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees the space between the parties as containing different responses to one address, not merely two names before an observer.
findings.containment: This is attributed HFT interpretation. Khabir and basir may state exhaustive knowledge without adjudicating uptake here; the finding does not assign either focus party to a contextual group or decide who is guided.

epistemic.reason: The listed coordinates and roots agree with 17:82-84 and the focus words khabir/basir, but the diagnostic link is an attributed HFT inference; target morphology is absent.

findings.title: The witness also holds the evidence's availability
findings.claim: Human knowledge is little, revelation can be withdrawn, and no independent guardian can prevent it; against that sequence, God's sufficiency as witness includes custody of the evidence people receive, whose continued availability is mercy.
findings.mechanism: Before, God is an informed observer of evidence shared by everyone. The context limits human knowledge in 17:85, makes the revealed word removable and denies an external wakil in 17:86, then names mercy in 17:87. Those conditions meet focus kafa and khabir; after, the witness is not merely observing a common archive but knows and controls whether the evidence remains available.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see the witness claim reaching the conditions under which revelation is known and retained.
findings.containment: This is an attributed contextual inference, not a claim that witnesshood lexically means preservation. The same verses may concern revelation's preservation without redefining shahid; the primary sufficiency and knowledge remain.

epistemic.reason: Context coordinates and roots match 17:85-87, and the focus return is explicit. The evidence-custody relation is attributed to a legacy-unbound HFT record.

findings.title: Unanswerability can itself function as testimony
findings.claim: The coalition's failure to produce a counterpart despite mutual backing, followed by varied examples and persistent refusal, can make the address itself an exhibited sign; God's witness then accompanies a claim already publicly answerable.
findings.mechanism: Before, the final witness adds external corroboration to an unsupported assertion. The focus shahid carries the sign-indicating branch while 17:88 supplies the maximal gathering, a matching counterpart as criterion, and mutual aid; 17:89 adds varied examples and refusal. Their contact turns the failed comparison into evidence that accompanies testimony.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see the recitation's public challenge as part of what is witnessed, not only as a claim awaiting an outside witness.
findings.containment: This is an exploratory, attributed HFT inference. The inability to produce a like is the challenge stated in 17:88; whether that itself activates the focus sign facet remains uncertain. It may be a separate sign while 17:96 names only God's personal knowledge.

epistemic.reason: The surface coordinates and roots agree, and the focus has an exact sign-indicating branch option. The HFT contact between failed imitation and witnesshood is unusual and remains attributed rather than lexically established.

findings.title: The witness relocates the terms of proof
findings.claim: The escalating requests for a spring, a falling sky or face-to-face display, an ascent, and a personally readable book meet God's sufficiency and sight; adequacy moves from spectacles the challengers prescribe to the witness who sees them.
findings.mechanism: Before, divine witness might look like one more item that could satisfy a demand for proof. The 17:90, 17:92, and 17:93 conditions prescribe visible events and access on the challengers' terms; focus kafa and basir answer with sufficiency and sight. The relation reverses who controls the evidentiary scene: the witness already sees the challengers. The immediate human-messenger exchange remains a live, narrower referent.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees the catalogue as an effort to set conditions for proof and the answer as relocating adequacy to the one who sees both sides.
findings.containment: This is an attributed contextual reading, not a claim that 17:96 explicitly answers every demand in 17:90-93. The immediate human-messenger exchange in 17:94-95 may be the narrower referent. Kafa remains a sufficiency verdict and basir remains seeing.

epistemic.reason: Each HFT context coordinate and root matches the supplied surface; the focus words return explicitly. The broad connection to the whole demand sequence is attributed and is kept alongside the narrower 17:94-95 reading.

findings.title: The commanded saying is heard against little human knowledge
findings.claim: The HFT's attributed q-w-l/q-l-l contact lets the command qul be heard as an economical saying: little human knowledge meets the focus sufficiency verdict and divine inner expertise.
findings.mechanism: Before, the speaker seems to owe the dispute an ever larger explanatory proof. The focus command qul is linked by the supplied HFT split to qalilan in 17:85; that verse explicitly limits human knowledge, while focus kafa and khabir contrast an adequate appeal and full expertise. After, the compact command can perform epistemic restraint without changing its ordinary meaning.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can hear the commanded reply as proportionate to limited human knowledge, with sufficiency resting in the witness rather than in endless explanation.
findings.containment: This is exploratory attributed pressure, not a lexical gloss of qul. The QAC root is q-w-l while the source-analysis/HFT split reaches q-l-l; the primary reading remains simply 'say', and the bundle does not establish that the command is unusually brief.

epistemic.reason: The context coordinate q-l-l at 17:85:14 matches the supplied surface and the HFT trace returns to focus qul, kafa, and khabir. The focus carrier crosses a q-w-l/q-l-l split, so the relation stays attributed and exploratory.

findings.title: Sufficiency takes on an all-around field of sight
findings.claim: The gathered coalition and its mutual backing meet the focus branch image of people surrounding and looking; with basir and shahid in the same ayah, sufficiency can be pictured as an all-around field of observation rather than a numerical count of witnesses.
findings.mechanism: Before, one witness is merely numerically enough against a multitude. The focus kafa is attributed the surrounding-and-looking image, while 17:88 supplies a gathered coalition and mutual backing and focus basir supplies actual sight. Their contact makes the sufficiency spatial: a field of present observation that no coalition can reproduce.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can picture sufficiency as encompassing the scene, rather than as one witness counted against many.
findings.containment: This is exploratory and attributed. The branch is a mapped k-f-f image carried through a k-f-y focus reference; it is not the direct lexical meaning of kafa. The claim does not say that 17:88 explicitly describes people surrounding God or that a crowd physically escapes divine sight.

findings.claim: The external worship-and-help request in 1:5 activates the worship specialization of 17:96's 'His servants'; under this recitation lens, the people God knows and sees include worshippers asking for aid.
findings.mechanism: The focus carrier is the possessed plural ibadihi. The independent external trigger is the first-person plural naabudu/nastaeen in 1:5. Their contact changes the phrase from a general class of servants into a devotional community that worships and seeks help, without identifying that community with either side of the focus dispute.
findings.reader_payoff: A reciter can locate themselves among the servants who worship and ask for help, and hear the focus knowledge-and-sight clause as including that devotional dependence.
findings.containment: This is a bounded external overlay on one focus word. It does not claim that the Fatiha's 'we' is the same as the focus's 'me' or 'you', or import the Fatiha's wider path or worship system into 17:96.

epistemic.reason: The same-root carrier and the explicit worship/petition act are supplied directly in the selected context projection. The reciter's inclusion and the bridge to the focus's disputants remain an interpretive lens, so pronoun identity is withheld.

branch_activations.facet_statement: Eylem, sıradan itaati aşan bir boyun eğme ve alçalma tutumu içerir.
branch_activations.carrier: The focus noun ibadihi names the people belonging to God as His servants; this core carries submission to a master.
branch_activations.independent_trigger: External 1:5 supplies the distinct first-person acts naabudu (we worship, word index 2) and nastaeen (we seek help, word index 4).
branch_activations.activation: The plural focus carrier meets the external worship-and-petition acts, so the servants under divine knowledge include a community actively submitting and asking for aid.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The focus servants can be heard, under this external recitation lens, as worshippers and petitioners whose inner reality and outward situation God knows and sees.
branch_activations.boundary: This overlay does not equate the Fatiha's first-person plural with either party in the focus dispute; it adds a devotional facet to the focus noun only.

branch_activations.facet_statement: Merkezî dinsel kullanım, Tanrı'ya yönelen tapınma ve kendini bu yönelişe vermedir.
branch_activations.carrier: The focus noun ibadihi is the carrier of the religious specialization in which servants direct worship to God.
branch_activations.independent_trigger: External 1:5 explicitly says 'You alone we worship' and 'You alone we seek help', an independent devotional act rather than a general mention of divinity.
branch_activations.activation: The explicit worship verb in 1:5 activates the religious specialization of focus ibadihi; the help-seeking clause makes the relation one of worshipping dependence, so khabir and basir address petitioners as well as disputants.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The servants described in 17:96 include, under this overlay, worshippers who seek aid from God.
branch_activations.boundary: This is a Fatiha overlay, not a claim that 17:96 quotes 1:5 or that its I/you pronouns refer to the same people. The primary meaning 'His servants' remains intact.
